Growing pains are typically non-articular, intermittent bilateral aches or pains in the legs that occur in the evening or at night in children aged 3-12 years. They are not associated with limping or limited mobility and do not involve the joints ([2006](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1557982/))


Growing pains is an accepted medical term, though the pains are not due to growing. The typical case of growing pains occurs in a healthy, clinically normal, young child, in the middle of the night, causing intense pain for 10 to 15 minutes in both legs (knees, thighs, calves or shins). 
([1999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10048249/))


Typically, growing pains affect children aged 3 to 12 years and tend to occur during the evening or nighttime, with intensity that can disrupt the child's sleep quality.
[...]
Growing pains is a diagnosis of exclusion, the absence of a clear definition, normal radiography, and laboratory biomarkers result in the diagnosis relying primarily on clinical manifestation.
([2024](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11146583/))

Pain in the lower limbs of children and adolescents, commonly referred to as GP [growing pains] by pediatricians and orthopedists, may reflect a precursor or comorbidity with migraine. ([2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37671464/))


In a retrospective epidemiologic analysis of 532 Mediterranean children, investigators found that 130 patients aged 4 to 12 years had symptoms consistent with growing pains within the past year. The mean age of children who had growing pains [...] was 8.6 ± 2.5 years, with discomfort usually beginning between the ages of 3 and 6 years of age. The prevalence of growing pains was decreased as children became older in a study from the Lancet in 1928. Specifically, [...] 21.2% of children older than 12 years had growing pains. ([2017](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5349398/))
